title: ALMA views a stellar explosion in Orion
caption: Debris from an explosive star birth in the Orion Molecular Cloud, imaged by ALMA, Gemini South and ESO's Very Large Telescope
celestial: OMC, Orion Molecular Cloud · constellation Orion · about 1400 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO), J. Bally/H. Drass et al.

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This composite view of the Orion Nebula complex captures firework-like debris, with the well-known Trapezium Cluster of hot, young stars near the bottom. The debris is what remains of an explosion some 500 years ago, set off as a group of massive stars was being born.

Stellar explosions usually bring to mind supernovae, the violent deaths of stars. These new ALMA observations show that the other end of a star's life cycle, its birth, can also be violent and explosive.

The colours in the ALMA data come from carbon monoxide gas and encode motion through the Doppler shift. Blue marks gas rushing toward us at the highest speeds, while red marks gas approaching more slowly. The Doppler effect changes the wavelength of light from a moving source, so it reveals how fast gas is moving along our line of sight.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (4.02 x 4.20 arcminutes) and distance (1400 light years), the frame spans roughly 1.6 × 1.7 light-years. Its light set out about 1,400 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: ALMA's millimetre observations of carbon monoxide are colour-coded by speed: blue for gas approaching fastest, red for gas approaching more slowly. The background is optical and near-infrared imaging from Gemini South and the VLT.
filters: 1.64 μm · Infrared Fe II (Gemini Observatory GSAOI)
1.25 μm · Infrared J (Very Large Telescope ISAAC)
1.65 μm · Infrared H (Very Large Telescope ISAAC)
2.2 μm · Infrared Ks (Very Large Telescope ISAAC)
1.3 mm · Millimeter 216-233 GHz (Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array Band 6)
understand.eye: The millimetre-wavelength and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the blue and red here encode speeds, not colours anyone would see.

explore: The background combines optical and near-infrared images from the Gemini South telescope and ESO's Very Large Telescope, and the ALMA data do not cover the whole frame. The Orion Molecular Cloud lies about 1400 light-years away.
alt: A composite view of part of the Orion Nebula complex with blue and red firework-like debris and a cluster of stars towards the bottom.
